name: Juche
info: Juche, the Juche idea, is the official ideology of North Korea and its ruling Workers' Party of Korea; it stresses human independence and consciousness, national self-reliance and loyalty to the leader, and it took shape from 1955 under Kim Il Sung.

facts.thinkers: Kim Il Sung, to whom North Korean sources attribute it; Hwang Jang-yop, his top adviser on philosophy, whom Western scholars generally credit with its conceptualisation and early development; Kim Jong Il, who declared it a distinct ideology in the 1970s and developed it further; Kim Jong Un, who succeeded him
facts.texts: Kim Il Sung's speech “On Eliminating Dogmatism and Formalism and Establishing Juche in Ideological Work” (1955), the “Juche speech”; his 1967 speech to the Supreme People's Assembly on independence, self-sustenance and self-defence; the Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System (1974); Kim Jong Il's On the Juche Idea (1982)
facts.ideas: the masses of the people as the masters of the revolution and its motive force; political independence (chaju); economic self-sufficiency (charip); military self-reliance (chawi); the primacy of ideology and political consciousness; the leader at the centre of the masses (suryong); opposition to reliance on great powers (sadae)
facts.today: It is the official ideology of North Korea and the Workers' Party of Korea, in the form of Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism until the party's 9th Congress in 2026 removed that name from its rules; abroad it has been adopted or studied by small parties and groups, such as the Nepal Workers' and Peasants' Party

t: Juche holds that the masses of the people are the masters of the revolution and that a country prospers once it achieves political, economic and military self-reliance, which North Korea's government pursued from the 1950s.

In the famine of 1994 to 1999 estimates of the dead range from 240,000 to 3,500,000, and the UN commission of inquiry of 2014 found violations by the state, including prison camps and executions, that the government rejects.

Scholars disagree about what Juche is: Brian Reynolds Myers likens it to Japanese fascism and ultranationalism, Charles K. Armstrong calls it a quasi-religion, and Derek R. Ford stresses its continuity with Marxism–Leninism.
dyk: Juche was a word of German philosophy before it was a doctrine: it was coined in Japan in 1887 to translate Subjekt, and North Korean editions of Marx used it even before 1955. The Juche calendar counts years from 1912, the year of Kim Il Sung's birth.
ev: Kim Il Sung gives the “Juche speech”, the first documented reference to Juche as an ideology

Kim Jong Il introduces Kimilsungism and the Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System

A UN commission of inquiry publishes a 400-page report on human rights in North Korea; the government rejects its findings

sections.origins:
Official statements by the North Korean government attribute the origin of Juche to Kim Il Sung's experiences in the Down-with-Imperialism Union during Korea's liberation struggle against Japan. The first documented reference to Juche as an ideology dates to 1955, when Kim Il Sung delivered a speech titled “On Eliminating Dogmatism and Formalism and Establishing Juche in Ideological Work”. The speech promoted a political purge similar to the Yan'an Rectification Movement in China and became known as the “Juche speech”.

The word comes from the Sino-Japanese 主體, coined in 1887 to translate the concept of Subjekt in German philosophy into Japanese. It migrated to Korean around the turn of the century with that meaning and appeared in Japanese translations of Karl Marx. North Korean editions of Marx used the word even before it was attributed to Kim Il Sung in its supposedly novel meaning in 1955.

Western scholars generally agree that Hwang Jang-yop, Kim Il Sung's top adviser on philosophy, was responsible for the conceptualisation and early development of Juche. Hwang rediscovered the speech in the late 1950s, when Kim Il Sung, having established a cult of personality, sought to develop his own version of Marxism–Leninism and solidify his position in the Workers' Party of Korea. Andrei Lankov argues that the first reference to Juche as an ideology came on 14 April 1965, in a speech Kim gave in Indonesia, and that the 1955 speech used the word in a different meaning.
sections.ideas:
According to Naenara, North Korea's official web portal, Juche means that the masses of the people are the masters of the revolution and construction and also its motive force. It incorporates the historical materialist ideas of Marxism–Leninism but emphasises human agency, the role of political consciousness and the primacy of ideology and propaganda. Its goal is a self-reliant state that determines its political, economic and military affairs independently.

Three principles carry this goal. Political independence (chaju) means equality and mutual respect among nations and the right of every state to self-determination; it is set against sadaejuui, reliance on a great power, though Juche does not advocate total isolation and encourages cooperation between socialist states. Economic self-sufficiency (charip) is held to be required for political independence; in On the Juche Idea Kim Jong Il argued for an independent national economy based on heavy industry. Military self-reliance (chawi) calls for a domestic defence industry, and Kim Jong Il held that allies' military aid is effective only if the state is strong in its own right.

The theory of Suryong makes the leader central. Where Marxism–Leninism sees the material conditions of production as the driving force of history, Juche takes human beings to be the driving force, but holds that the masses need the leadership of a great leader. Its summary is that the popular masses are placed in the centre of everything and the leader is the centre of the masses. The theory describes the leader as a flawless human being who never makes mistakes.
sections.spread:
Juche was first regarded as a variant of Marxism–Leninism. In the 1970s Kim Jong Il declared it a distinct ideology, and as he emerged as Kim Il Sung's likely successor loyalty to the leader was increasingly emphasised, as expressed in the Ten Principles for the Establishment of a Monolithic Ideological System, introduced in 1974 together with Kimilsungism. Kim Jong Il said in 1976 that Marxism–Leninism had become obsolete and that Kimilsungism could not be explained within its frameworks.

In the 1980s and 1990s Kim Jong Il made further breaks from Marxism–Leninism while insisting that Juche inherits it. In 1982 he stated that love for the nation came before love for socialism, and in 1990 he introduced Socialism of Our Style. Songun, military-first politics, was first mentioned in 1997 and credited to Kim Jong Il as the next stage of Juche; in late 2021 Kim Jong Un declared that it would be replaced by “people-first politics”. After Kim Jong Il's death in December 2011 Kimilsungism became Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism, adopted in April 2012 as the party's only guiding idea.

Outside Korea Kim Il Sung promoted Juche in the Third World as an anti-imperialist ideology. The first International Scientific Seminar on the Juche Idea met in Antananarivo from 28 to 30 September 1976, with participants from more than 50 countries, and in 1978 North Korea founded the International Institute of the Juche Idea in Tokyo. Juche study groups formed abroad, and in South Korea a faction of the student movements of the 1980s, the Juche faction or Jusapa, embraced it as an alternative to the country's political system.
sections.power:
Juche has been the official ideology of North Korea and its ruling party. After the devastation of the Korean War the state rebuilt its economy on heavy industry, aiming at the greatest possible self-sufficiency, and developed what has been called the most autarkic industrial economy in the world. The Korean People's Army is one of the largest on earth and has developed its own nuclear missiles.

The pursuit of self-sufficiency met its limits in the famine of 1994 to 1999, which the government called the Arduous March. Less than 20% of the country's mountainous terrain is arable, and the country had never been self-sufficient in food; several experts considered it unrealistic and economically imprudent for it to aim at self-sufficiency rather than trade. When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, aid and cheap oil ended and energy imports fell by 75%. Floods in 1995 and 1996 and a drought in 1997 followed, and the public distribution system, in which foreign observers said food went to people according to their political standing and loyalty to the state, failed. Estimates of the death toll vary widely: between 240,000 and 3,500,000 of about 22 million people died of starvation or hunger-related illness, with deaths peaking in 1997. Amnesty International found in 2004 that the government's policy prevented the swift and equitable distribution of aid and that its actions had exacerbated the effects of the famine.

In February 2014 a UN commission of inquiry, chaired by Michael Kirby, published a 400-page report based on first-hand testimony and found systematic, widespread and gross violations, many of which in its words constitute crimes against humanity. The commission was refused access to the country. The government called the inquiry a political plot and rejected the findings as a product of the politicisation of human rights, and it has said that its constitution guarantees human rights, that these are strictly enforced and that reports of abuses in prison camps are false.

The internment camps for political offences, run by the state security department, are estimated to hold 80,000 to 120,000 prisoners. Former prisoners and guards report forced labour, torture and public executions. Most inmates are reported to arrive without trial.

Movement and speech are controlled. Citizens need a permit to travel outside their county, leaving the country without permission is punished, and refugees returned from China are reported to be beaten and sent to camps. The government's position, put through the Korean Central News Agency, is that international criticism is a pretext for overthrowing its Juche-based system.
sections.critiques:
Critics have called Juche a nationalist ideology and a departure from Marxism–Leninism. Brian Reynolds Myers argues that it has more in common with Japanese fascism and ultranationalism than with Marxism–Leninism. Charles K. Armstrong holds that North Korea may appear “Stalinist in form” but is “nationalist in content”, and Shin Gi-wook that its government stresses the Korean people's blood, soul and national traits, supports social hierarchy rather than a classless society, and places ideology above materialism. Derek R. Ford, by contrast, emphasises its continuity with Marxism–Leninism and credits it as the principle that let North Korea survive the collapse of the Eastern Bloc.

A few critics dismiss the idea that Juche is an ideology at all. Myers says it has no underlying belief system and exists to be praised and not read; Alzo David-West calls it “meaningless on logical and naturalistic grounds”; Robert E. Kelly argues that it exists solely to protect the Kim family's monopoly over political power.

Armstrong calls Juche a quasi-religion and argues that familism became a political religion in it, with Kim Il Sung as the father of the people; Byung Ho Chung and Heonik Kwon liken the commemorations of the Kim leaders to Confucian ancestor worship. Western Marxists have called the cult of personality non-Marxist and undemocratic.

Stephan Haggard and Marcus Noland, Amnesty International and others hold the government responsible for the severity of the famine. North Korea rejects all such reports and calls the defectors who give testimony agents of an anti-North agenda.
sections.legacy:
Juche remains the official ideology of North Korea. Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism, which the party's 4th Conference of April 2012 declared its only guiding idea, was removed from the Rules of the Workers' Party of Korea at the 9th Congress in 2026. North Korea's official portal describes the state as independent and socialist, guided by Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism.

Juche has been taken up outside North Korea. The Black Panther Party of the United States studied it in the 1960s and 1970s. In 2014 the secretary-general of the Nigerian–DPRK Friendship Association, Alhassan Mamman Muhammed, claimed there were thousands of adherents in Nigeria, and the Nepal Workers' and Peasants' Party declared Juche its guiding idea in 2016. Far-left and far-right organisations have adopted or studied it, among them, reportedly, a neo-Nazi group and the Rural People's Party, an affiliate of the Order of Nine Angles. The Albanian leader Enver Hoxha called Kim Il Sung's attempts to spread Juche in the Third World “pretensions”.

Comparisons have been drawn with other doctrines. Park Sang-seek finds rhetorical similarities with Syrian Ba'athism, though Juche has in his view a stronger ideological basis. Its concept of a sacred leader has been compared to the State Shinto of Imperial Japan, in which the Emperor was seen as a divine being.

summary: Juche is the official ideology of North Korea, first documented in Kim Il Sung's 1955 speech. It holds that the masses are masters of the revolution and that a state must be politically, economically and militarily self-reliant, and it gives the leader a central role. A famine struck North Korea in 1994 to 1999, and a UN commission of inquiry reported prison camps and executions, which the government rejects. Scholars dispute whether it is Marxism, nationalism or a quasi-religion.
references: Bruce Cumings, Korea's Place in the Sun: A Modern History (W W Norton and Company, 1997)
Andrei Lankov, The Real North Korea: Life and Politics in the Failed Stalinist Utopia (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Brian Reynolds Myers, The Cleanest Race: How North Koreans See Themselves and Why It Matters (Melville House, 2011)
Gi-wook Shin, Ethnic Nationalism in Korea: Genealogy, Politics, and Legacy (Stanford University Press, 2006)
Dae-sook Suh, Kim Il Sung: The North Korean Leader (Columbia University Press, 1988)
notes: Start 1955, circa true: the first article gives the 1955 speech as the first documented reference; Andrei Lankov places the first reference to Juche as an ideology in 1965 and says the 1955 speech used the word in a different meaning. Both are given in the text.

Revised with two further articles (1990s North Korean famine, Human rights in North Korea): the power section now tells the famine, the commission of inquiry, camps, executions and controls as those articles do, each attributed. One takeaway, two key events (1994–1999, 2014), the summary and the closing critiques paragraph were added; nothing else changed.

The famine article does not itself attribute the famine to Juche; it names economic mismanagement, loss of Soviet support, floods and drought, sanctions and the inflexible planned system. Only the experts' view that self-sufficiency was unrealistic, and the first article's remark that autarky has been blamed, link it to the ideology. The text does not claim more.

The rights article's own framing: it says North Korean human-rights theory is based on Marxist theory, Confucian tradition and the Juche idea, and that the government calls criticism a pretext to overthrow its Juche-based system. Both are given as attributed.

Death figures: 240,000 to 3,500,000 and the 2011 U.S. Census Bureau 500,000 to 600,000 are from the famine article; the rights article also gives 240,000 to 420,000 from census-based estimates and Rigoulot's 100,000 executions, 1.5 million camp deaths and 500,000 famine deaths. Rummel's figure was left out. Camp populations: 80,000 to 120,000 (rights article) and about 200,000 by 2017 (Amnesty and the U.S. Committee); the 40% malnutrition death figure is given as an estimate without a named source in the article.
The 2014 report year and the 2013 execution of Jang Song-thaek are as the rights article gives them. The 1994 to 1999 span is the famine article's.

The 1956 purge sentence was moved from the second paragraph of power into the first; no content lost. The 2026 removal of Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism from the party rules is as the first article states it.
The article has no reference list in the saved text, so references is empty.

Left out: the Arirang Festival and ritual passages, the Songun details of the 1999 editorial, military technical details, Rummel's totals, abductions, religion, disability and women's sections of the rights article, and the post-2000 food situation.
